probe: Before the next playable prototype, headless/browser game evaluation, devlog, or cross_review note, did I write a 3-5 milestone oracle trace or expected shortest success path before adding reflective advice?

For each failed run used as evidence, did I assign exactly one primary failure_type among perception, reasoning, execution, latency, or not_observed, and preserve the observation/run/seed or route that supports it?

If reflection suggests a fix, did I freeze one next experimental condition for retry, such as same seed, same route, same milestone, or same input script, and label any unsupported reflection as reflection_pollution_unverified or taxonomy_overreach?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two game/headless/cross_review notes already include a short oracle trace, one primary failure_type per failed run, and a fixed retry condition before reflective advice changes design or acceptance criteria.

change.summary: Added a reversible GameVerse-inspired failure-typing probe: write a 3-5 milestone oracle trace, tag failed runs as perception/reasoning/execution/latency/not_observed, and freeze one retry condition before letting reflection alter a game design.

reviews.title: HarnessFix: trace-grounded agent harness failure diagnosis and scoped repair
reviews.reason: Score 17. HarnessFix is useful now because Codex game and phase work often treats a failed browser/headless/probe run as either model weakness or a generic workflow issue. Existing probes ask for state traces, branch checks, observability layers, and failure types, but they do not force the repair target to be separated among game code, test harness, probe script, prompt/instruction, logging, or orchestration. Keep this as a reversible failure-log probe scoped to playtest/probe failures, not an automated repair loop or broad HTIR adoption.
probe: Before the next failed playable prototype, browser/headless game evaluation, canvas/DOM probe, Slack/memory automation probe, or phase-quality validation note, did I name the failed_step that exposed the problem, such as input action, screenshot, state dump, tool call, validator, finalization, or scheduled script step?
Did I record expected_effect and observed_effect as a concrete state delta or missing artifact, instead of accepting success status, no console error, or a prose failure label as the whole evidence?

Before choosing a fix, did I assign one primary harness_layer and repair_scope among game code, test harness, probe script, prompt/instruction, logging, orchestration, or external dependency, and mark unresolved cases as harness_anchor_unverified or repair_scope_unclear?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two failed playtest/probe/automation validation notes already name failed_step, expected versus observed effect, and a primary harness_layer plus repair_scope before changing code, prompts, or acceptance criteria.

change.summary: Added a reversible HarnessFix-inspired failure-log probe: failed runs must name the responsible step, expected/observed state effect, and repair scope before selecting a fix.

reviews.title: Algorithmic collusion meta-game lens for Log/Mir/Ash instance divergence
reviews.reason: Score 15. This shared-read is useful now because Codex phase work can read Log/Mir/Ash or multi-agent outputs as independent evidence while those outputs may share prompts, memory, phase incentives, and Slack-visible priors. Existing coordination probes ask for private views and handoff evidence, and observability probes ask for layer boundaries, but neither directly asks whether apparent agreement is independent convergence or shared-prior echo before using it as design or memory evidence. Keep this reversible and scoped to multi-instance reviews, cross-instance summaries, and shared-reads disagreement analysis, not a durable collusion benchmark or permanent instance policy.
probe: Before the next Log/Mir/Ash comparison, cross-instance review, multi-agent evaluation, or shared-reads disagreement note, did I name the shared priors that could make agreement non-independent, such as same source article, phase prompt, AGENTS rules, memory atom, Slack directive, or recent staging note?

Did I preserve one independent signal or divergence axis before treating agreement as evidence, such as distinct raw source, different test route, separate failure observation, contrary interpretation, or label agreement_shared_prior when no independent signal exists?

If the conclusion changes memory, candidate priority, game acceptance, or a Slack-facing judgment, did I choose one transfer mode among independent_convergence, shared_prior_echo, useful_disagreement, needs_third_signal, or no_update?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two multi-instance or cross-review notes already name shared priors, preserve an independent signal or divergence axis, and label whether agreement should change action or stay no_update.

change.summary: Added a reversible algorithmic-collusion-inspired multi-instance agreement probe: name shared priors, preserve independent divergence evidence, and label whether agreement is independent convergence or shared-prior echo before changing action.

reviews.title: CommonRoad-Game: human operation logs as reproducible scenario and regression assets
reviews.reason: Score 16. CommonRoad-Game is useful now because Codex game work can still treat manual play, human feel checks, or one-off browser interactions as ephemeral evidence. Existing D2E, quality-workflow, and harness probes already cover synchronized event streams, provenance, and repair scope, but they do not directly ask whether a valuable human/manual interaction becomes a replayable scenario fixture with an oracle for future regression. Keep this reversible and scoped to playable prototype and game-evaluation notes, not a permanent simulation framework rule.
probe: Before the next manual playtest, human feel check, browser interaction, or playable prototype evaluation where a human-operated run matters, did I preserve the minimal scenario fixture needed to replay or approximate it, such as build/version, seed, route, starting state, input script, level id, or relevant config?

Did I attach one regression oracle to the captured interaction, such as expected checkpoint reached, collision avoided, item collected, time band, failure reproduction, UI state, or player-facing cue observed, instead of leaving it as a prose impression only?

If the interaction cannot be replayed, did I label the gap as scenario_fixture_missing, oracle_missing, manual_only_evidence, or regression_unavailable before using it to change design, acceptance criteria, memory, or future tests?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two manual-playtest, human-feel-check, browser-interaction, or playable-prototype evaluation notes already preserve a minimal replayable scenario fixture, attach one regression oracle, and label unreplayable evidence before changing design or acceptance criteria.

change.summary: Added a reversible CommonRoad-Game-inspired human-operation-to-regression probe: turn valuable manual interactions into minimal scenario fixtures with one oracle, or label the evidence as manual-only/unreplayable.

reviews.title: CausalGame: interactive causal-reasoning benchmark for AI Scientist agents
reviews.reason: Score 17. CausalGame is useful now because Codex playable-diff and memory-routing work can still treat a good outcome, successful route, or frequently recalled atom as evidence that the underlying mechanism was understood. Existing probes cover trace rows, branch checks, harness anchors, and human-operation fixtures, but they do not directly split outcome score from causal explanation or check for post-hoc causal stories after a lucky run. Keep this reversible and scoped to game evaluation, shared-read candidate evaluation, and memory-routing notes rather than adopting a full causal benchmark.
probe: Before the next playable diff, headless/browser game evaluation, shared-read candidate pass decision, or memory-routing note, did I separate the observable outcome from the claimed mechanism, such as clear rate versus route understanding, recall frequency versus utility, or candidate interest versus production relevance?

Did I name at least one possible bias or confounder behind the outcome, such as seed, route selection, spawn luck, UI measurement error, hidden state, evaluator prompt, tag frequency, or source recency, instead of treating the strongest correlation as causal evidence?

Before changing design, acceptance criteria, posting priority, or memory structure, did I preserve one intervention, counterexample, alternate seed, ablation, evidence table row, or label the claim as causal_explanation_unverified or outcome_only_success?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two game-evaluation, shared-read candidate, or memory-routing notes that make causal claims already split outcome from mechanism, name a possible confounder, and preserve an intervention/counterexample or explicitly label causal uncertainty before changing practice.

change.summary: Added a reversible CausalGame-inspired outcome/explanation split probe: distinguish outcome metrics from causal mechanism claims, name possible confounders, and require an intervention/counterexample or uncertainty label before using success as design or memory evidence.

reviews.title: X official MCP server as a replacement candidate for fragile Twitter input channels
reviews.reason: Score 17. This shared-read is useful now because Codex/Log phase work depends on external input channels such as X/Twitter scraping, jina/WebFetch fallbacks, Slack ingestion, and MCP/API candidates, but can drift from a concrete channel failure into a generic integration project. The transferable point is narrower than the existing MCP responsibility-boundary probe: before replacing an input path, preserve the failure pressure, constrain the operation subset and cost/write surface, and define fallback or rollback conditions. Keep this reversible and scoped to external input-channel migrations, not a standing instruction to adopt X MCP.
probe: Before the next external input-channel change, such as X/Twitter ingestion, MCP/API replacement, browser scraping fallback, RSS/search connector, or Slack-derived ingestion path, did I name the current failure pressure with evidence such as error code, blocked URL, timeout, stale response, T_response delay, missing source class, or repeated manual workaround?

Did I constrain the proposed path to a minimal operation subset and name any excluded generic surface, such as read-only search/timeline/bookmarks versus write/post/link-post, instead of wrapping every available API or tool operation by default?

Before implementation or recommendation, did I name the cost/write/auth/security boundary and one fallback, rollback, or approval gate, or label the proposal channel_migration_unverified before using it to change scripts, memory routing, Slack posting, or phase expectations?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two external input-channel migration notes already preserve failure evidence, constrain operation subset and excluded surfaces, and name cost/write/auth/security plus fallback or approval gates before changing scripts, routing, posting, or phase expectations.

change.summary: Added a reversible X-MCP-inspired input-channel migration probe: record concrete failure pressure, keep the replacement to a minimal operation subset, and name cost/write/auth/security plus fallback or approval gates before changing ingestion or posting paths.

reviews.title: Coachable agents for interactive gameplay
reviews.reason: Score 17. This atom is useful now because Codex game work can still judge bot, enemy, NPC, or headless agent behavior by task success, clear rate, or crash-free execution while missing whether the run followed the intended play style. Existing probes cover failure type, scenario replay, causal explanations, and harness repair, but not the narrower split between task_success and style_adherence or the paired-run check where only the style flag changes. Keep this as a reversible game-agent evaluation probe, not a mandate to add RL, UVFA, or a durable style taxonomy.
probe: Before the next bot, enemy, NPC, companion, racing, combat, or headless game-agent evaluation, did I name one runtime style flag or behavior mode being tested, such as aggressive, defensive, safe, fast, readable, supportive, cinematic, pressure, or restraint, instead of judging only task success?

Did I record task_success and style_adherence as separate evidence fields, such as clear rate, time, damage, survival, or objective completion versus distance kept, retreat timing, repetition rate, screen obstruction, pressure window, support interference, or readability cue?

If the style claim changes design, acceptance criteria, or memory, did I preserve a paired run, same seed, same route, same scenario, or mark style_tradeoff_unverified when only prose impression or one aggregate score exists?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two bot/enemy/NPC/headless-agent evaluation notes already name a style flag, separate task_success from style_adherence, and preserve a paired run or explicitly label style trade-off gaps before changing design or acceptance criteria.

change.summary: Added a reversible Coachable Agents-inspired game-agent style probe: name the intended behavior mode, separate task success from style adherence, and keep a paired-run or same-scenario comparison before treating bot/NPC behavior as design evidence.

reviews.title: Seduced by the Narrative: rhetorical injection against LLM game adjudicators
reviews.reason: Score 16. This shared-read is useful now because Codex game work may use LLM GM, NPC, rule-explanation UI, natural-language command parsing, or memory/directive text where fluent, plausible prose can be mistaken for rule-valid state transition evidence. Existing probes cover narrative graph state, AI-native state transitions, causal explanations, and failed-run taxonomies, but not the narrower separation between rhetorical quality and mandatory mechanical checks. Keep this reversible and scoped to free-text game adjudication and persuasive memory/directive inputs, not a permanent rule to harden every narrative exchange.
probe: Before the next LLM GM, narrative NPC, rule-explanation UI, natural-language command parser, or persuasive Slack/memory directive evaluation, did I separate rhetorical quality from mechanical validity instead of letting fluent or plausible prose stand in for a rule check?

Did I name the mandatory rule gate or state-transition predicate that must survive the prose, such as required roll/check, resource cost, hidden-information boundary, inventory/key condition, cooldown, safety rule, or current directive precedence?

If a free-text claim changes game state, memory priority, posting eligibility, or acceptance criteria, did I preserve one neutral or adversarial variant, such as authority, pseudo-logic, omission, or emotionally persuasive wording, or label the claim rhetorical_injection_unverified before adopting it?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two free-text game-adjudication, narrative-NPC, command-parser, or persuasive memory/directive evaluations already separate rhetorical quality from mechanical validity, name a mandatory rule gate, and preserve or label one rhetorical variant before changing state, memory, posting, or acceptance criteria.

change.summary: Added a reversible Seduced-by-the-Narrative-inspired rhetorical-injection probe: separate prose quality from mechanical validity, name the mandatory rule gate, and preserve or label one persuasive variant before accepting free-text claims.

reviews.title: ToolBench-X: recoverable tool-environment hazards and valid recovery paths
reviews.reason: Score 17. ToolBench-X is useful now because Log_cdx phase work and playable-diff validation still mostly confirm clean paths: server starts, browser opens, canvas is nonblank, Slack returns ts, memory recall prints output. Recent probes anchor failed steps and responsibility boundaries, but they do not ask for one deliberately recoverable hazard with a predeclared recovery path before calling a harness robust. Keep this as a reversible harness/phase probe, scoped to tool boundaries, not a broad mandate to inject failures everywhere.
probe: Before the next browser, build/test, Slack posting, memory recall, file-ingest, or playable-diff validation change where I claim the harness or workflow is robust, did I name exactly one recoverable hazard type among specification_drift, invocation_error, execution_failure, output_drift, or cross_source_conflict?
Did I write the valid recovery path before testing or changing the workflow, such as retry with changed timeout, fallback source, parser tolerance, source-of-truth precedence, or stop-with-evidence?

If the hazard appears during the run, did I record hazard_type, recovery_action, and verdict as recovered, unrecoverable, recovery_path_missing, or clean_path_only instead of only noting flaky failure or success?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two harness/phase/playable-diff validation notes that mention tool failure, browser automation, Slack posting, memory recall, build/test, or source conflict already classify recoverable hazards, predeclare a recovery path, and record recovery verdicts without expanding permanent rules.

change.summary: Added a reversible ToolBench-X-inspired recoverable-hazard probe: for one tool/harness boundary, classify the hazard, predeclare the recovery path, and record the recovery verdict before claiming robustness.

reviews.title: A-TMA: state-aware memory roles for ghost-memory failures
reviews.reason: Score 17. A-TMA is useful now because Codex phase work repeatedly uses old shared-reads, directives, candidates, staging notes, and prototype feedback where an old record may be historically valid but invalid for current judgment. Existing probes cover load strategy, recall utility, lifecycle triggers, and anti-bloat validation, but they do not directly ask whether the retrieved record is current, historical, transition, superseded, or draft-only before using it. Keep this as a reversible state-role probe for memory cleanup, recall, candidate lifecycle, and game-spec feedback, not a durable schema migration or full ATMA overlay.
probe: Before the next memory cleanup, recall summary, shared-reads candidate lifecycle decision, directive lookup, or game-spec feedback reuse, did I label the retrieved record role as current, historical, transition, superseded, draft_only, or role_unknown?

Did I keep current-judgment evidence separate from historical or transition evidence, and preserve at least one source_ts, ruleset_id, candidate status, supersedes link, or staging permalink that justifies the role?
If the role is ambiguous, did I avoid using the record as current policy or design evidence and mark state_role_unverified, ghost_memory_risk, or transition_link_missing?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two memory-cleanup, recall, candidate-lifecycle, directive-lookup, or game-spec feedback notes already separate current, historical, transition, superseded, and draft-only records before changing memory, posting priority, or prototype acceptance.

change.summary: Added a reversible A-TMA-inspired state-role probe: label recalled records as current, historical, transition, superseded, draft-only, or unknown before using them as policy, candidate, memory, or game-spec evidence.

reviews.title: Goodbye Postmortems, Hello Critical Stage Analysis
reviews.reason: Score 16. This atom is useful now because Codex phase and game work can still put lessons into final summaries, diaries, or archives after the artifact is effectively closed. Critical Stage Analysis transfers as a narrower reversible check: name the current stage, capture one written feedback item that can still change the next action, and label archive-only feedback instead of turning it into another durable rule. Existing probes cover milestone acceptance and quality feedback routes, but not the stage-timed question of whether feedback is still actionable before closure.
probe: Before the next cycle phase closure, playable diff acceptance, game evaluation, or memory cleanup where lessons may be left as a final summary, did I name the current stage and one decision the feedback can still change?
Did I capture one written feedback item as keep, change, or question with evidence and a target next action, instead of only archiving it as diary, postmortem, or retrospective prose?

If the feedback cannot affect the current artifact or next stage, did I label it archive_only, next_stage_input, no_actionable_stage, or stage_unknown before adding rules, probes, or broad process changes?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two cycle phase closures, playable-diff acceptances, game evaluations, or memory cleanup notes already name the active stage, route at least one written feedback item to a next action, and label archive-only feedback before adding durable rules or probes.

change.summary: Added a reversible Critical Stage Analysis-inspired feedback-routing probe: before closing a phase or playable milestone, name the current stage, route one written feedback item to a decision it can still change, and label archive-only feedback instead of promoting it to rules.

reviews.title: ClassicLogic: compositional generalization benchmark for logic puzzles
reviews.reason: Score 17. ClassicLogic is useful now because Codex game and candidate-evaluation work can still collapse difficulty, article quality, or playtest success into a single pass/fail result. The transferable point is narrower: name the required primitive strategies, check their composition depth, and record the first missing layer when a puzzle, tutorial, headless run, or shared-reads candidate fails. Existing probes cover outcome/mechanism splits and harness failure anchors, but not strategy hierarchy or failure-layer attribution. Keep this reversible and scoped to puzzle/tutorial/headless/candidate-evaluation notes, not a general rule for all game design.
probe: Before the next puzzle, tutorial, logic mechanic, headless game evaluation, or shared-reads candidate gate where success or quality may be compressed into pass/fail, did I name the required primitive strategies or quality layers, such as recognize_entity, build_relation, apply_local_rule, combine_constraints, plan_sequence, overview_density, method_understanding, evaluation_understanding, application_design, or limitation_analysis

Did I separate primitive-layer success from composition-depth success, such as single mechanic versus two-constraint combination, isolated clue versus relational graph, or article summary versus method-plus-evaluation understanding?

If the artifact fails or is postponed, did I record the first missing layer or label it strategy_layer_unverified, composition_depth_unclear, or pass_fail_only_evidence before changing design, acceptance criteria, posting priority, or memory structure?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two puzzle/tutorial/headless/candidate-evaluation notes already name required primitive strategies or quality layers, distinguish primitive success from composition depth, and record the first missing layer instead of only pass/fail or postpone.

change.summary: Added a reversible ClassicLogic-inspired composition-layer probe: name required primitive strategies or candidate quality layers, distinguish primitive success from composition depth, and record the first missing layer before design, posting, or memory changes.

reviews.title: GPTNT: asymmetric-information KTANE benchmark for multimodal cooperative agents
reviews.reason: Score 13. GPTNT is relevant to game/harness evaluation because it combines asymmetric information, live countdown, free-text communication, GUI grounding, multi-turn state, and recovery after failure. The actionable lesson would be to separate role-private observations, communication turns, and final operations in cooperative evaluations. However the current state already has overlapping probes for multi-agent coordination, role assignment, communication bottlenecks, action/reason/message splits, shared priors, manual replay fixtures, and social counterpart traces. Adding another communication-role probe would mostly restate existing checks, so this cycle records the read and rejects adoption to avoid probe bloat.

change.summary: Marked GPTNT as reviewed and rejected because existing coordination and communication probes already cover the actionable behavior.

reviews.title: GameEngineBench: runtime-integrated patch evaluation for UE5 game projects
reviews.reason: Score 17. GameEngineBench is useful now because Codex playable-diff work can still stop at build success, canvas nonblank, or the directly edited feature working, while missing runtime integration regressions in neighboring state, lifecycle, UI, restart, timer, score/resource, or scene transitions. Existing probes cover failed-step anchoring and harness repair scope, but not the narrower build-to-runtime integration gate after a local game-code edit. Keep this as a reversible playable-diff validation probe, not a durable UE-specific rule.
probe: Before the next playable diff, browser/headless game validation, or game-code patch acceptance, did I separate build/launch evidence from runtime integration evidence instead of treating compile, server start, canvas nonblank, or no console error as enough?

Did I run or define one fixed input trace or scenario lasting roughly 30-90 seconds and record snapshots for the edited feature plus at least two neighboring systems such as player state, enemy lifecycle, UI/HUD, timer, score/resource, scene transition, restart, persistence, or input focus?

If only the directly edited behavior was checked, did I label the result integration_regression_unverified, trace_missing, neighbor_state_unchecked, or launch_only_evidence before changing acceptance criteria, memory, or Slack-facing claims?
reviews.withdrawal_condition: Drop this probe if the next two playable-diff or browser/headless game-validation notes already separate launch/build evidence from runtime integration evidence, preserve a fixed input trace or scenario with neighboring-system snapshots, and label unverified integration gaps before accepting the change.

change.summary: Added a reversible GameEngineBench-inspired runtime-integration probe: after build/launch, validate a fixed trace against the edited feature plus neighboring game systems before treating a playable diff as accepted.

active_probes.scope: next theme variant, reskin, generated-asset pass, asset-linked playable diff, or small prototype where Codex may change surface assets and labels around an existing game loop
questions: Before the next theme variant, reskin, asset-linked playable diff, or generated content pass where I change visuals, labels, lore, UI text, prompts, or audio direction around an existing game loop, did I name the fixed gameplay contract and the editable asset slots separately?

Did I use or sketch one compact theme manifest with setting, location/environment, key nouns, palette/readability constraints, and reusable naming terms, then derive the affected slots from it instead of hand-editing unrelated surface details?

Before calling the variant coherent or playable, did I check slot completeness, proper-name consistency, visual/readability constraints, and the usual build/runtime playability evidence separately from aesthetic preference?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two theme-variant, reskin, generated-asset, or asset-linked playable-diff notes that mention fixed mechanics, editable slots, theme manifests, naming consistency, readability, generated visuals, labels, lore, UI text, or runtime playability.

active_probes.scope: next gameplay video, screenshot sequence, browser-use or Playwright trace, replay, or headless playtest failure where Codex may call something a bug, glitch, broken interaction, visual defect, or runtime defect from weak evidence
questions: Before the next gameplay video, screenshot sequence, browser-use/Playwright trace, replay, or headless playtest failure where I call something a bug, glitch, broken interaction, or visual/runtime defect, did I record the smallest temporal span or step range where the defect starts and ends instead of only a final screenshot or pass/fail?

Did I write expected state versus observed state and one plausible normal-gameplay explanation to reject, so unusual but valid mechanics, animation, camera, UI, pause, or transition states are not mislabeled as defects?

If the same phenomenon appears multiple times, did I group it as one event with multiple spans or reproduction points, and label the likely layer as physics/collision, rendering, animation, input/control, UI/state, progression/quest, performance/timing, or harness artifact before changing prompts, memory, rules, or code broadly?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two gameplay-video, screenshot-sequence, browser-use/Playwright, replay, or headless playtest failure notes that mention bugs, glitches, visual/runtime defects, temporal spans, step ranges, expected-vs-observed behavior, normal explanations, recurrence, or harness artifacts.

active_probes.scope: next multi-agent, NPC-party, cross-instance, Slack-handoff, or headless coordination evaluation where Codex may judge team quality from individual progress, final success, or plausible conversation alone
questions: Before the next multi-agent, NPC-party, cross-instance, Slack-handoff, or headless coordination evaluation where I judge team quality, did I separate individual/base progress from coordination outcomes such as handover success, synchronization delay, role collision, duplicate work, or unmet dependency?

Did I record one tiny ablation or contrast such as communication on/off, shared memory on/off, explicit role assignment on/off, or same-seed solo versus team run before changing prompts, rules, memory, or harness structure?

If the result is weak, did I label the failure layer as base competence, communication, shared memory, reasoning/plan horizon, role assignment, observation mismatch, timing, or environment objective design before making a broad coordination claim?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two multi-agent, NPC-party, cross-instance, Slack-handoff, or headless coordination notes that mention individual progress, team quality, communication, shared memory, role assignment, handoff, synchronization, duplicate work, unmet dependencies, or coordination failure layers.

active_probes.scope: next new playable diff, board/tabletop-like prototype, or rule-heavy game mechanic where Codex may move from theme or idea directly to implementation or broad prose review
questions: Before the next new playable diff, board/tabletop-like prototype, or rule-heavy game mechanic where I move from theme or idea to implementation, did I leave a short design draft with theme, player verb, win or failure condition, one-minute change, and intended player judgment?
Did I run critique as localized defects with layer, severity, target, repair suggestion, and accept/reject or comparison, instead of adding only broad self-review prose?
If I use persona or audience feedback, did I mark it as a pre-playtest prediction and name which real runtime or human-play evidence is still needed before treating the design as validated?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two new playable diffs, rule-heavy prototypes, or board/tabletop-like design notes that mention ideation, rule drafts, defects, repair suggestions, persona feedback, runtime evidence, or playtest validation.

active_probes.scope: next game-agent, headless playtest, solver, or benchmark-like note where Codex may generalize from one game, genre, or prototype into a broad agent-capability claim
questions: Before the next game-agent, headless playtest, solver, or benchmark-like note where I claim agent capability, did I name the tested capability such as planning, memory, reflection, tool use, perception, control, adaptation, or environment interaction instead of reporting only win or completion?

Did I state whether the task is same-game practice, same-genre transfer, held-out game transfer, or only a local prototype check, and avoid presenting an in-distribution result as cross-game evidence?
If the evaluation uses one game or one prototype, did I record one likely missing capability or genre axis that would remain untested before changing prompts, memory, or harness policy?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two game-agent, headless-playtest, solver, or benchmark-like notes that mention capability, win/completion, planning, memory, reflection, tool use, perception, control, same-game practice, same-genre transfer, held-out game transfer, or untested genre axes.

active_probes.scope: next playable-diff failure review, memory-routing change, shared-reads gate, evaluator tweak, or phase-process change where Codex may judge an improvement only from final artifact quality or final score
questions: Before the next playable-diff failure review, memory-routing change, shared-reads gate, evaluator tweak, or phase-process change where several components could be fixed, did I list 3-5 candidate components and rank the top 3 before applying the first change?

Did I write one sentence for why the top-ranked component is likely causal, naming the observed failure signal and the expected intermediate improvement instead of relying on final score or final post quality alone?
After the change, did I record whether the ranking was supported, contradicted, or unresolved, and keep non-chosen candidates visible rather than rewriting history around the chosen fix?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two playable-diff failure reviews, memory-routing changes, shared-reads gates, evaluator tweaks, or phase-process changes that mention candidate components, priority ranking, final score, final post quality, causal rationale, or intermediate evidence.

active_probes.scope: next procedural level generation, generated map/mission/room, PCG-like content, or level-evaluation note where Codex may treat one score, screenshot, or pass/fail as overall level quality
questions: Before the next procedural level generation, generated map/mission/room, PCG-like content, or level-evaluation note, did I name the exact evaluation claim: solvability/functionality, difficulty, player experience, visual/naturalness, diversity, controllability, comparison to prior content, or domain transfer?
Did I match the claim to the evidence method, metric, comparison point, and game domain instead of letting one fitness score, screenshot, or pass/fail stand for overall level quality?

If the generator/domain is too novel for a fair quantitative comparison, did I narrow the claim to a system description, small verifier, or reusable evaluation artifact rather than forcing a misleading benchmark-style score?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two PLG, generated-level/content, or map/mission evaluation notes that use solvability, difficulty, player experience, diversity, controllability, comparison, domain transfer, screenshots, fitness scores, or pass/fail evidence.

active_probes.scope: next rule-discovery puzzle, tutorialized mechanic, or LLM player-proxy evaluation where Codex may treat rule explanation as enough evidence of executable understanding
questions: Before the next rule-discovery puzzle, tutorialized mechanic, or LLM player-proxy evaluation, did I state whether the examples make the intended rule identifiable, including at least one varying or contrastive case when needed?

Did I separate rule verbalization from execution by recording whether the agent/player can describe the hidden rule, choose the needed item/action for a new case, and perform the ordered action sequence without brute-force exploration?
If the task has no hidden rule or tutorial learning step, did I mark this probe not applicable rather than expanding it into a general game-evaluation rule?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two rule-discovery puzzle, tutorial, or LLM player-proxy evaluation notes that include examples, hidden rules, rule descriptions, action traces, or efficient execution claims.

active_probes.scope: next AI advisor, NPC dialogue, negotiation/copilot, recommendation/search summary, or agent-output evaluation where Codex may judge a message without naming sender/receiver payoff mismatch or information granularity
questions: Before the next AI advisor, NPC dialogue, negotiation/copilot, recommendation/search summary, or agent-output evaluation where the speaker may have a goal different from the user/player, did I name the sender goal, receiver goal, and the likely bias direction instead of judging only truthfulness or style?

If the message is costly to verify or unverifiable in the moment, did I classify whether it over-reveals, under-reveals, rounds information into a coarse interval, or withholds key state before trusting or tuning the dialogue/agent?
If sender and receiver interests are aligned or the task is not an advisor/dialogue/evaluation situation, did I mark this probe not applicable rather than expanding it into a general distrust rule?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two advisor/dialogue/evaluation tasks that involve possible preference mismatch, unverifiable messages, NPC guidance, negotiation, recommendations, search summaries, or agent output with its own objective.

active_probes.scope: next game implementation or playable-diff patch where Codex may add boolean flags, mode variables, one-off conditions, or exception branches to satisfy incremental behavior
questions: Before the next game implementation or playable-diff patch that adds a boolean flag, mode variable, one-off condition, or exception branch, did I name the underlying state as player-facing game state, transient presentation/effect state, harness/test state, or modeling debt?
If the condition changes gameplay, did I check whether the player can observe the state through UI, animation, rule feedback, or level layout rather than only through hidden code flags?

If two or more new flags interact, did I either collapse them into a small explicit state machine/table or record why a local exception is cheaper for this prototype and should expire after the next verification?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two game implementation or playable-diff patches that add flags, modes, conditions, exception branches, state machines, or player-readable state feedback.

active_probes.scope: next shared-reads candidate selection, game prototype comparison, memory-cleanup priority decision, or evaluation summary with more than two candidates
questions: Before the next shared-reads candidate selection, game prototype comparison, memory-cleanup priority decision, or evaluation summary with more than two candidates, did I name at least two preference clusters or use-contexts before choosing a winner?
Did I check whether any candidate outside the aggregate top choice has strong support for one cluster such as immediate probe, memory redesign, game feel, safety, or long-term principle?
If I still collapse to one decision, did I record the kept top-k or the cluster-specific reason for not keeping a lower aggregate candidate?

active_probes.scope: next game-agent evaluation, playable-diff verification, or phase outcome where Codex may treat knowledge, explanation, short-run success, or benchmark-like score as evidence of long-horizon action capability
questions: Before the next game-agent evaluation, playable-diff verification, or phase outcome where I cite a model/prototype's knowledge, explanation, short-run success, or benchmark-like score, did I name one action-level trajectory signal that shows the knowledge was used under changing state?

If the agent or prototype can explain the rule but fails in play, did I classify it as a knowing-doing gap and record the observed transition where knowledge stopped becoming action, instead of treating it as generic reasoning failure?

If only static explanation or short interaction evidence is available, did I label the conclusion as static/short-horizon and name the missing long-horizon trajectory evidence before changing game rules, harnesses, or memory directives?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two game-agent evaluations, playable-diff verifications, or phase outcome notes that use knowledge claims, explanations, short-run success, benchmark-like scores, action trajectories, or long-horizon capability claims as evidence.

active_probes.scope: next memory schema, atom/index field, recall-output label, or memory_redesign change where Codex may add persistent fields before proving that a judgment word changes behavior
questions: Before the next memory schema, atom/index field, recall-output label, or memory_redesign change, did I name the candidate judgment word and the existing signal that may already approximate it, such as score, source_ts, validation deadline, lifecycle status, related/conflict note, or human feedback log?

Did I test the word first in recall or staging output and record one concrete decision it changed, such as deprioritize, verify-before-use, link-as-conflict, keep-as-hypothesis, or promote-to-action, before making it a persistent field?
If no concrete decision changes, did I keep the idea as local vocabulary and avoid adding schema, index, directive, or AGENTS/phase-prompt text?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two memory schema, recall-output, atom/index-field, or memory_redesign notes that propose candidate judgment vocabulary, new fields, index metadata, directives, or phase-prompt text.

active_probes.scope: next memory/state structure change, recall-index edit, atom promotion, compression note, or memory-tree consolidation step where Codex may improve memory without naming temporal scope, representation, and control policy
questions: Before the next memory/state structure change, recall-index edit, atom promotion, compression note, or memory-tree consolidation step, did I name the memory unit on three axes: temporal scope, representational substrate, and control policy?

If I propose a new field, index, directive, or lifecycle change, did I state whether it changes what is stored, how it is represented, or when it is written/read/merged/forgotten, instead of treating all memory improvement as one action?
Did I keep this as descriptive structure first and avoid adding automation, thresholds, or persistent rules unless a concrete failure trace requires them?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two memory/state structure or recall-index notes that change fields, indices, directives, compression, promotion, or lifecycle behavior.

active_probes.scope: next level, map, route, mission, puzzle, resource-placement, or traversal-generation task where Codex may treat one start-to-goal path as proof that generated content is playable
questions: Before the next level, map, route, mission, puzzle, resource-placement, or traversal-generation task, did I check more than one start-to-goal solution path and name at least one reachable mid-state or off-path state that must still be recoverable?

If a route succeeds, did I avoid calling the content safe until I considered softlock risks from optional branches, one-way movement, consumable resources, timing windows, enemy/object state changes, or player deviation from the intended path?

If recoverability is uncertain, did I keep the result as a candidate and name the smallest deterministic check, scripted detour, reachability query, or manual trace needed before promoting it as playable content?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two level/map/route/mission/puzzle or traversal-generation notes that use solvability, reachability, scripted paths, resource placement, one-way movement, or route validation as evidence.

active_probes.scope: next playable-diff review, game-evaluation note, shared-reads candidate gate, or memory-quality claim where Codex may give a broad single-agent review without actively attacking one hidden failure condition
questions: Before the next playable-diff review, game-evaluation note, shared-reads candidate gate, or memory-quality claim, did I name one hidden target or failure condition that should be attacked rather than only summarized?

Did I split the check into attacker, defender, and judge roles for one short round: attacker tries to induce or expose the failure, defender proposes the smallest defense or revision, and judge decides using a concrete log, file diff, route, candidate text, or stated evidence pointer?
If judge evidence is missing or the target is vague, did I keep the result as an open risk or candidate probe instead of claiming the artifact, post, or memory change is better?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two playable-diff, game-evaluation, shared-reads candidate-gate, or memory-quality notes that judge an artifact, post, or memory change.

active_probes.scope: next Phase Game Start, playable diff, game-evaluation note, or prototype repair where Codex may judge game quality using code-like compile/run, screenshot, or headless feedback
questions: Before the next Phase Game Start, playable diff, game-evaluation note, or prototype repair, did I name which feedback loop I am optimizing: compile/runtime correctness, headless regression, visual inspection, route behavior, human play feel, or design hypothesis exposure?
Did I state whether that feedback is immediate and granular or delayed, sparse, subjective, and interaction-dependent before treating it as evidence of game quality?

If only code-like feedback is available, did I limit the claim to implementation readiness or structural regression and name the smallest next play-facing observation needed before calling the game better?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two game-start, playable-diff, or game-evaluation notes that use compile/run, screenshot, headless, route, or human-play evidence.

active_probes.scope: next game tuning note, playable diff, self_judgment table, phase outcome score, or evaluation summary where Codex may add, average, rank, or compare numeric parameters before checking whether the quantity is additive
questions: Before the next game tuning note, playable diff, self_judgment table, or phase outcome score that adds or aggregates numbers, did I label each key quantity as extensive, intensive, ratio, rank, or judgment score?

For any intensive, ratio, rank, or judgment quantity, did I name the composition rule before using it, such as weighted average, max/min, threshold, condition-specific comparison, vector direction, or non-additive qualitative judgment?

Before claiming improvement from a larger total, did I check whether the total only increased an extensive surface measure while the intended intensive player experience, design direction, or evaluation confidence stayed unchanged?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two game-tuning or evaluation notes that aggregate numeric quantities or self-judgment scores.

active_probes.scope: next level, enemy-placement, room-connection, reward-item, or hazard generation/repair pass where Codex may ask one broad generator or one aggregate score to judge the whole playable artifact
questions: Before the next level, enemy-placement, room-connection, reward-item, or hazard generation/repair pass, did I split the change into at most three local editing passes instead of asking one broad generator to optimize the whole map at once?

Did each local pass name the shared deterministic proxy it is allowed to improve, such as unreachable tile count, start-to-goal distance, local enemy-density gradient, recovery-point risk distance, or invisible instant-death placement count?
Before calling the result better, did I check that the proxy is not being treated as fun, tension, or readability itself and name the remaining human/browser/headless evidence needed?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two level-generation or generated-layout repair notes that use local editing passes, deterministic proxies, or generated map quality claims.

active_probes.scope: next Phase 1 external intake, Phase 2 shared-reads analysis, game-design idea note, or memory/action handoff where Codex may preserve a future idea without connecting it to a concrete next action
questions: Before the next Phase 1 external intake, Phase 2 shared-reads analysis, or game-design idea note that preserves a future idea, did I attach it to exactly one target project or phase output instead of leaving it as a general inspiration?
Did I name the minimal next action and evidence pointer for the idea, such as candidate note, staging section, playable diff probe, search keyword experiment, or evaluation fixture?
Did I check whether the idea is advancing the current goal or merely optimizing the intake/search/evaluation machinery, and keep it local or defer it if it risks means-ends reversal?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two Phase 1 or Phase 2 notes that create future-idea seeds or convert external shared-reads into project actions.

active_probes.scope: next game evaluation, playable diff, automated playtest, headless/browser verification, or prototype self-judgment where Codex may treat one run or one route as closed-world pass/fail evidence
questions: Before the next game evaluation, playable diff, automated playtest, or headless/browser verification, did I label each claim's oracle type as binary, statistical, or interpretive instead of forcing every result into pass/fail?

Did I record at least one behavior-characterization note, such as outcome distribution across seeds/routes, repeated failure condition, state cluster before failure, monotony condition, or interesting unexpected behavior?
If only one run or one route exists, did I limit the conclusion to the observed condition and name the next selective exploration condition rather than claiming general quality or coverage?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two game-evaluation or playable-diff notes that use headless, browser, automated playtest, or route evidence.

active_probes.scope: next game evaluation, playable diff, automated playtest, browser/headless verification, or manual-play note where Codex may use one route, trace, or success rate as representative player evidence
questions: Before the next game evaluation, playable diff, automated playtest, or browser/headless verification, did I label each route with the player profile it approximates, such as novice confusion, competent survival, expert optimization, random stress, scripted regression, LLM rule-clarity, or manual feel?
Did I record the movement or input pattern assumptions for that profile instead of treating a single action trace, route, or success rate as representative of human play?

If the build is intended to serve multiple skill levels, did I avoid a global quality verdict until at least one contrast route, seed, scenario, or human observation checks whether the mechanic still works across profiles?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two game-evaluation or playable-diff notes that use automated, scripted, random, LLM, or manual routes as player evidence.

active_probes.scope: next game prototype, template extraction, playable diff, or game_templates_design update where Codex may copy a genre skeleton as fixed content instead of converting it into pressure budget and variation knobs
questions: Before the next game prototype, template extraction, or playable diff, did I express the genre skeleton as pressure budget, role slots, or state-transition constraints instead of a fixed content or placement list?
Did I name at least one invariant that must survive variation and one knob that may vary with seed, player state, tempo, or difficulty?
If I cannot map the skeleton to pressure budget or variation knobs, did I keep the source as reference material instead of turning it into an implementation rule or template?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two game prototype or template-extraction notes that reuse a genre skeleton, design skeleton, or game template.

active_probes.scope: next playable prototype review, headless trace summary, game-design self-judgment, or completion report that claims tension, frustration, relief, mastery, confusion, rhythm, or player experience quality
questions: For the next playable prototype review or headless trace summary, did I list 3-5 concrete gameplay events before naming any player emotion or experience label?

For each selected event, did I write the appraisal hypothesis as a falsifiable mapping such as threat, agency, relief, loss, surprise, mastery, or confusion, instead of treating it as proven human feeling?
Did I keep the appraisal timeline separate from the final fun or quality verdict, using it only to choose one next design question, contrast run, or manual-play focus?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two playable prototype reviews or headless trace summaries that make player-experience claims.

active_probes.scope: next long Codex cycle log, game bot episode, phase incident, completion report, or agent/bot failure classification where surface success/failure may hide observed belief, expected action, or deviation structure
questions: When reviewing the next long Codex cycle log, game bot episode, phase incident, or completion report, did I name what the actor had observed or could reasonably believe at the key decision point?
Did I state the expected action under the user goal or game objective before labeling the actual action as bug, rule misunderstanding, exploration miss, reward hack, or agent drift?
Did I run a brief verify/refine pass that looks for evidence against the first suspicion, so recalled guardrails do not become automatic over-detection?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next two long-log or game-bot reviews where behavior is classified from trajectory evidence.

active_probes.scope: next memory ingest, consolidation, recall, staging summary, or long-lived memory edit where a memory artifact may be trusted or rewritten without naming the failure stage
questions: For the next memory ingest, consolidation, recall, or staging-summary decision, did I classify the main risk stage as ingestion poisoning or context loss, consolidation semantic drift, or retrieval conflict/hallucination?

Did I preserve one evidence pointer appropriate to that stage, such as raw Slack JSONL/source_ts for ingestion, before/after text or diff for consolidation, or query plus competing atom ids for retrieval?
If the failure stage is unclear, did I keep the change to state/staging or a reversible probe instead of rewriting MEMORY, atoms, directives, or long-lived summaries?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next memory ingest, consolidation, recall, staging summary, or long-lived memory edit that depends on trusting or rewriting memory artifacts.

active_probes.scope: next ADV / mystery / conversation-choice prototype brainstorm, LLM-as-player game concept, or game-memory conversion where an external article may be saved without becoming a reusable design check
questions: Before treating a source as useful memory, did I convert it into one production-time question tied to a concrete stuck point, such as first clue, hint timing, partial credit, search burden, or chapter-end confirmation?
Did I state which forced-judgment burden the design device relaxes: ability, exploration,??, or retry cost, instead of only naming a reference game or article?
If the memory cannot affect the next playable diff or brainstorm decision, did I leave it as a candidate/reference instead of promoting it to a playbook, directive, or broad rule?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next ADV/mystery brainstorm, LLM-as-player concept, or external-article-to-playbook memory conversion.

active_probes.scope: next game/headless evaluation or playable diff where a mechanic, scoring change, or player-facing feedback may be judged only by pass/fail, clearRate, or a single verdict
questions: Before reporting improvement, did I name the answer-check timing: immediate, batched, end-of-run, or human review?

Did I include one near-miss or partial-progress signal instead of collapsing the result to pass/fail, such as N of M goals met, distance to target, wrong-category count, or representative failed policy?
Did I state one anti-bruteforce or anti-overfit boundary so the partial signal cannot be gamed by the evaluation policy alone?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next game/headless evaluation or playable diff that reports a mechanic or scoring change.

active_probes.scope: next playable diff / headless game evaluation / cross_review bug or design-quality judgment where a symptom may be mistaken for a verified finding
questions: Before calling a headless/game-eval finding verified, did I write the minimal reproduction condition: initial state, action sequence, expected result, and observed result?
If only a symptom or anomaly was observed, did I label it as suspected rather than verified and choose the next smallest action to reproduce or falsify it?
Did the log, packet, or staging note preserve enough state/action trace for another agent or Nao_u to replay the finding without relying on my interpretation?
active_probes.expires_after: Review after the next playable diff, headless game evaluation, or cross_review bug/design-quality judgment.

active_probes.scope: next cycle staging / shared-reads post / memory or game evidence update where output volume may be mistaken for a real change in judgment, implementation, or verification
questions: 今回増えた surface は何か: 投稿、staging、state、atom、ログ、スクリーンショット、表のどれかを1つ名指ししたか。
対応する substrate は何か: 次回の判断、実装ゲート、検証方法、検索語、撤退条件のどれが変わったかを1行で書いたか。
surface だけが増えた場合、恒久ルール追加ではなく、削る・延期する・次の最小確認に閉じる、のどれかを選んだか。
active_probes.expires_after: 次に cycle staging、shared-reads 投稿、memory/game evidence 更新のいずれかで成果を報告した 1 回で見直す。

active_probes.scope: next shared-reads self-feedback / memory improvement / probe or directive adoption where a candidate conveniently supports an existing belief or workflow
questions: 採用理由を書く前に、この atom が既存方針を気持ちよく補強しているだけではないかを疑い、反証候補または採用しない理由を1つ置いたか。
反証候補を見てもなお採用する場合、採用先を恒久ルールではなく probe / metric / state のどれに狭めるかを明示したか。
反証で弱くなった場合、無理に統合せず defer / reject として reviewed だけを残す判断を許可したか。
active_probes.expires_after: 次に shared-reads 自己フィードバック、memory 改善案、または probe/directive 採用判断を1回行った後に見直す。

active_probes.scope: next memory / directive / AGENTS / phase prompt persistent writeback
questions: この差分は、確認を省く条件・Slack/tool/git の既定動作・自律実行範囲のどれかを広げていないか。
core state に相当する AGENTS.md、active directive、phase prompt への変更なら、raw/candidate/probe で済む内容を昇格していないか。
危険度が不明な場合、削除ではなく保留・staging 記録・ユーザー確認に落とせるか。
active_probes.expires_after: 次回 Phase 4c または次の恒久 state 更新 1 回で見直す

active_probes.scope: next game-dev / agent-improvement cycle result judgment
questions: このサイクルの主要成果は、内省やルール解釈ではなく、外から再実行できる diff、smoke、測定ログのどれかに接続しているか。
game/* を触った場合、最低 1 つの deterministic 確認と、必要なら stochastic な観察ログを分けて残したか。
記憶整理・Slack投稿・日記だけで終わる場合、それを成果ではなく harness 未達として staging に明記できているか。
active_probes.expires_after: 次回 Phase 4a/4c または次のゲーム制作サイクル 1 回で見直す

active_probes.scope: next game prototype headless/self-judgment use
questions: ヘッドレス結果を設計判断に使う前に、その harness は人間プレイで問題になった状態や目標状態へ到達できているか。
到達できていない場合、設計を変えるのではなく harness 未達として扱い、観測ログ・到達条件・次の最小修正を分けて残したか。
人間プレイ依存を減らす目的が、未検証の自動測定を権威化する方向へすり替わっていないか。
active_probes.expires_after: 次に headless/self-judgment をゲーム設計判断へ使う 1 回で見直す
